---
title: "R practice sandbox"
subtitle: "Predict, repair and interpret short examples before revealing the answers."
---

## 1. Read the pipeline

```r
analysis_data <- patients |>
  select(age, treatment, outcome) |>
  filter(age >= 18, !is.na(outcome))
```

What changes: rows, columns, or both?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

Both. `select()` retains three columns, and `filter()` retains only adults with recorded outcomes.

</details>

## 2. Repair the missing-value filter

```r
complete_data <- patients |>
  filter(outcome != NA)
```

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

```r
complete_data <- patients |>
  filter(!is.na(outcome))
```

`NA` represents an unknown value and must be checked with `is.na()`.

</details>

## 3. Predict the summary shape

```r
patients |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(
    patients = n(),
    mean_age = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

How many rows should the result contain?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

One row per observed treatment category. `group_by()` changes the level at which `summarise()` calculates.

</details>

## 4. Spot the selection error

```r
adults <- patients |>
  select(age >= 18)
```

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

`select()` chooses columns, not observations. Use:

```r
adults <- patients |>
  filter(age >= 18)
```

</details>

## 5. Choose the plot

You want to compare the distribution of recovery time across three treatment groups. Which is the best starting plot?

A. Bar chart of recovery time  
B. Boxplot or violin plot by treatment group  
C. Pie chart  
D. Scatterplot with patient ID on the x-axis

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

**B.** Recovery time is continuous and treatment is categorical. A boxplot provides compact group summaries; a violin plot or points can add distributional detail.

</details>

## 6. Interpret a coefficient

```r
model <- lm(systolic_bp ~ age_years, data = patients)
```

The age coefficient is 0.55. What does it mean?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

In the fitted sample, each additional year of age is associated with an estimated 0.55 mmHg higher mean systolic blood pressure, assuming a linear relationship. It does not show that ageing alone caused the difference.

</details>

## 7. Interpret an odds ratio

An adjusted logistic model reports an odds ratio of 0.70 for intervention versus usual care.

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

Holding the included covariates constant within the model, the estimated odds of the event in the intervention group were 0.70 times those with usual care—a 30% lower odds. It is not automatically a 30% lower risk.

</details>

## 8. Find the reproducibility problem

```r
training_rows <- sample(1:nrow(data), 800)
```

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

The random split will change between runs unless a seed is set immediately beforehand:

```r
set.seed(2026)
training_rows <- sample(seq_len(nrow(data)), 800)
```

The split proportion and rationale should also be recorded.

</details>

## 9. Improve the conclusion

> “There was no association because p = 0.08.”

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

Report the effect and interval. For example: “The estimated association was [value] with a 95% CI from [lower] to [upper]. The interval includes no association and [any important effect], so the data are inconclusive rather than evidence of no association.”

</details>

## 10. Debug the model

```r
model <- glm(
  outcome ~ age + treatment,
  data = patients
  family = binomial()
)
```

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

A comma is missing after `data = patients`:

```r
model <- glm(
  outcome ~ age + treatment,
  data = patients,
  family = binomial()
)
```

</details>

## Build your own challenge

Take one code-along pipeline and:

1. explain every line in plain English;
2. predict the dimensions of each intermediate object;
3. deliberately introduce one syntax error and one reasoning error;
4. diagnose and repair both;
5. write a complete interpretation of the final output.
